hooks: Flat fact: Apple researchers strapped a Mac mini to a humanoid robot, and it walks into rooms it has never seen.
Collision: This robot never saw a real home in training. Then it got 91% right in six of them.
One-two: About 300 hours of fake rooms, and a real robot sits on a real chair.
Odd detail: The robot's brain is a Mac mini in a backpack.
What you'd assume: You'd think a robot needs people acting out every move. Apple's didn't.
spine: A robot trained only in generated rooms works in real ones, run from a Mac mini, but it still needs a person to write each task.
firstFrame: A Mac mini on a humanoid robot's back, with the line: never saw a real home in training.

scenes.narration: A humanoid robot from Apple's researchers never saw a real home while it learned. Then it walked into six real places nobody had mapped.
scenes.onScreen: Never saw a real home in training

scenes.narration: In Apple's own tests of single skills, it succeeded in 91% of 360 tries, with an M4 Pro Mac mini on its back doing the planning.
Normally a person acts out every move by hand, so an hour of robot data costs at least an hour of a person's time.
scenes.onScreen: 1 hour of data = 1 hour of a person

scenes.narration: Apple generated most of the motion data instead: about 300 hours of movement, in 1,000 computer-made rooms.
The plan comes from the Mac mini itself, through an A.I. model called Qwen, with no internet needed.
scenes.onScreen: Qwen, running on the Mac mini

scenes.narration: But chain tasks together, and success drops to a 70% average, tested in one room. A person still writes the prompt for every new task. And the paper reports no comparison with other published systems.
If this holds up, robot training could wait less on people's hours, and more on computers.
